author: Mark Atwood
text:
Crypto-security supplement (review-readonly) — completed.

**Findings filed:** t307.15 (P1, Section C, unbounded recursion in part_to_jmap_inner), t307.16 (P2, Section C, README How-to-use copy hazard missed by t307.2), t307.17 (P3, Section G+C, guessable blob-id construction in example/README/bench/rustdoc).

**Section-by-section confidence:**

- **Section A (key material lifecycle):** ~2 min. N/A — crate handles no key material; S/MIME / PGP explicitly out of scope per README §143-146. No findings expected; none filed. **Confidence high.**

- **Section B (side-channel hygiene):** ~2 min. N/A — no secret-dependent branches, indices, or compares in adapter, bench, or example. No findings expected; none filed. **Confidence high.**

- **Section C (untrusted input at protocol boundaries):** ~25 min. Read the full bench (384 lines), example (53 lines), README (168 lines), src/lib.rs (458 lines), and the relevant ~200 lines of mime-tree-0.3.0 parse.rs + part.rs::find_by_id to verify upstream recursion bounds (there are none). Two findings filed (t307.15 P1, t307.16 P2). **Confidence high on the recursion finding (verified all three recursive surfaces — `build_part`, `part_to_jmap_inner`, `find_by_id` — are unbounded). Confidence medium on whether other malformed-input vectors exist that the diff exercises:** I did not exhaustively map mime-tree's panic surface on adversarial inputs (oversized declared boundary, malformed quoted-printable, charset trouble in `decode_body_value`), and the adapter's filter_map paths at src/lib.rs:138/145/152 iterate over mime_tree-owned Vec<String>s whose memory bounds I did not verify. Probability another C-class finding lurks: ~15%. Would raise confidence if: a downstream `/do-beads` session ran `cargo fuzz` against `message_to_jmap_body` with malformed RFC 5322 inputs and reported no panic / no UB / no excessive allocation under arbitrary input.

- **Section D (random source quality):** ~1 min. N/A — diff and adapter use no randomness. Criterion bench harness uses its own RNG internally but not for security-relevant output. No findings expected; none filed. **Confidence high.**

- **Section E (persistent storage of secrets):** ~1 min. N/A — crate is pure compute; no I/O. Consumers handle storage and bring their own secret-handling. No findings expected; none filed. **Confidence high.**

- **Section F (logging output safety):** ~5 min. Substantively N/A — crate has zero `tracing` / `log` call sites. The example uses `println!(\"first textBody value: {:?}\", jmap_val.value)` to print decoded body content to stdout for demonstration; in a clearly-labeled `examples/` artifact this is appropriate and not worth filing (would not survive a code review comment per workspace bikeshedding rule). The log-capture-test pattern from workspace AGENTS.md is also N/A — there is no logging surface to test. No findings filed. **Confidence high.**

- **Section G (algorithm and parameter choice):** ~10 min. The crate uses no crypto primitives directly. Edge case: blob-ID construction pattern shown across all four documentation surfaces (bench, example, README, rustdoc) is enumerable, and consumers using blobId-existence as access control inherit cross-user blob enumeration. One P3 finding filed (t307.17). **Confidence high** that this is the only G-class concern in scope; the crate does no other primitive selection.

**Diff vs unchanged code:** I read the full unchanged src/lib.rs because t307.15 (the P1) lives there — the diff's new bench file exercises the recursive walker on 5-level nesting, which is exactly the 'shared helper that the diff touches through' pattern the supplement Section 7 warns about. I read mime-tree's parse.rs::build_part and part.rs::find_by_id to verify the upstream-bound question; I did NOT read mail_parser's source (one layer further upstream) — its DoS posture is its own concern, but if mail_parser happens to limit nesting then t307.15's exploitability changes from 'guaranteed' to 'depends on mail_parser's limit'. Would raise confidence on t307.15's severity if: `cargo run --example parse_eml` on a hand-crafted 10000-level-deep multipart fixture either succeeded (proving the full pipeline is unbounded) or stack-overflowed (also confirming) — either outcome is informative.

**Probability I missed a P0:** ~3%. The crate is a thin field-rename adapter with no key material, no crypto primitives, no RNG, no persistence, no logging. The only realistic P0 class would be a memory-corruption or sandbox-escape primitive reachable from malformed MIME via `unsafe` code — and `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` at src/lib.rs:35 plus a check of the dev-deps (`criterion`, `serde_json`) closes that path. No P1 to schedule a deeper external review pass is needed.

**Probability I missed a P1:** ~12%. Driven mostly by the 'other malformed-input panic surfaces' uncertainty under Section C above. If the maintainer wants to drive this down further, a `cargo-fuzz` target against `message_to_jmap_body` is the highest-yield investment.

**Convergence:** crypto-security supplement is complete. Per supplement closing rule, JMAP-t307 epic lifecycle remains owned by the primary review (do not close from here).
